aib.problem.reticle: Each die is {area} mm², larger than the {max} mm² a scanner can print in one shot (its reticle). Shrink the math or the memory on the chip, or split the chip into more dies.
aib.problem.needs-interposer: Stacked memory (HBM) must sit beside the die on a slice of silicon, an interposer: choose a CoWoS package.
aib.problem.stacks: This package holds at most {max} stacks of memory.

aib.problem.dies.one: This package holds at most {max} die.
aib.problem.dies.other: This package holds at most {max} dies.

aib.problem.silicon: The dies and the memory need about {need} mm² of room; this package has {max} mm².
aib.problem.clock: No safe voltage reaches {f} GHz. Lower the clock.
aib.problem.no-memory: The chip has no memory beside it. Add at least one memory device.
aib.note.memory-bound: Memory-bound: the math waits for the weights most of the time. More or faster memory, or smaller weights, would raise the speed more than extra math.
aib.note.compute-bound: Compute-bound: the memory keeps up easily. More area for math or a faster clock would help.
aib.note.balanced: Well balanced: the math and the memory finish each step at about the same time.
aib.note.low-yield: Only {percent}% of the dies work. Smaller dies (chiplets) or an older, calmer process would cut the cost of each chip.
aib.note.power-close: The power is close to the limit; cooling will be tight.
aib.note.newest-node: A16 only entered production in late 2026: the newest process costs more and puts the date at risk.
aib.note.compiler: A matrix engine needs a strong compiler team (the people who turn programs into its instructions). Budget for software, as Google does for its TPUs.
aib.note.cpu-math: CPU cores give far less math per mm² than units built for matrices, which is why AI chips spend their area on matrix math.
aib.note.agents: The date is missed. AI design agents would pull the schedule in by several months.
aib.note.fp4: The chip cannot read 4-bit weights. They take half the bytes, which nearly doubles the speed of a chip that waits on its memory.
aib.note.hbm-share: The stacked memory is {percent}% of the cost. Memory, not logic, leads the bill of an AI chip.
aib.arch.gpu.d: Programmable cores with units for matrix math. Runs anything, and most software is written for it.
aib.arch.sys.d: Large fixed arrays that only multiply matrices, as in Google's TPU. More math per mm² and per watt, less freedom.
aib.arch.cpu.d: General cores that can run anything. Flexible, but far less math per mm².
aib.node.n5.d: In production since 2020: cheaper wafers, few defects.
aib.node.n3.d: The process most AI chips of 2024 to 2026 are made on.
aib.node.n2.d: Gate-all-around transistors, in volume since late 2025. Less power, dearer wafers, more defects.
aib.node.a16.d: Power fed from the back of the wafer, starting in late 2026. The least energy, the newest and the riskiest.
aib.dies.d: A larger die does more math, and one speck of dust kills more of it. Several smaller dies (chiplets) share the work.
aib.sram.d: Fast memory built into the die itself. It takes area and leaks a little power.
aib.f.d: A faster clock needs a higher voltage, and power rises with the square of the voltage.
aib.fp4.d: Let the chip compute with 4-bit numbers (FP4) as well as 8-bit ones: 4% more area, and weights half the size where the brief allows them.
aib.mem.lp.d: The memory of phones and laptops: cheap, low power, a narrow road (little bandwidth).
aib.mem.gd.d: Graphics memory, on the board around the package.
aib.mem.h3.d: HBM (high-bandwidth memory): memory chips stacked right beside the die. Needs a CoWoS package.
aib.mem.h4.d: The next stacks, new in 2026: more than twice the bandwidth, and dearer. Needs a CoWoS package.
aib.pkg.org.d: A cheap package like a phone chip's, for one die.
aib.pkg.fc.d: A big package for up to two dies. No stacked memory.
aib.pkg.cs.d: The dies and the memory sit side by side on a slice of silicon (an interposer): up to 2 dies and 6 stacks.
aib.pkg.cl.d: A larger interposer made of bridged pieces: up to 4 dies and 12 stacks.
aib.agents.d: Let AI agents write, check and lay out parts of the design, with people reviewing: about a quarter less design time.
aib.hint.infer: Start with the line that reads zero: where can a model this large live? Then ask the reviewer which side waits, the math or the memory, and feed that side. Every fix has a price; watch what it does to the other gauges.
aib.hint.phone: A phone has little power and little money. What is this chip carrying that one person's replies never use? And when the date is the last line missing, who could share the design work?
aib.hint.train: One die cannot be larger than the scanner's shot. When one die is not enough, how many can a package hold, and which package? A slower clock on more silicon can do more math for less power.
aib.note: A teaching model: the prices of wafers, memory and packages are rough public estimates, and the months are typical, not a quote.
game.ch.power-curve.goal: This chip starts at 3 GHz and 0.75 V, and takes about 51 W. Find the fastest clock that runs safely on less than half that power: 2.2 GHz or more, under 25.5 W.
game.ch.power-curve.why: Every switch that flips takes a sip of energy, and the sip grows with the square of the voltage. But a lower voltage makes the gates slower, so the clock has to slow down with it. That trade is why a chip cannot simply be run faster, and why every chip has to choose its place on the same curve.
grow.blk-power: a power meter beside the studio, where the clock and the voltage are chosen
game.ch.counter.goal: Clock a four-bit counter at the top speed its slowest path allows, with no wrong count, at two different processes. Then push on, and watch it break.
game.ch.counter.why: A tick of the clock is a promise: every signal will have arrived before the next tick. The longest chain of gates between two flip-flops decides how short a tick can be. No two gates come out identical, so designers add up the worst case and keep a margin. How much speed is that margin worth?
grow.gate-counter: four lamps in front of the studio that count in step with a clock
ckp.p.intro: The clock is the beat every part of a chip steps to: 3 GHz is three billion ticks a second. The voltage is how hard the supply pushes: more makes every gate switch faster, and costs more power.
ckp.p.aria: Power against the clock: {f} GHz at {v} V takes {w} W.
ckp.p.legend: Thin lines: one voltage each, ending where its gates are too slow for the clock. Thick line: the frontier, the least power each clock can run on. Dot: your chip.
ckp.p.runs: Runs. At {v} V the gates keep up with a clock of up to {f} GHz.
ckp.p.fails: Fails timing: the slowest path is longer than one tick. This clock needs {v} V.
ckp.p.beyond: Beyond this chip's limit: no voltage it can take makes the gates fast enough.
ckp.p.hint: Power follows the voltage squared, so the voltage is where the saving is. But the gates slow as it drops. Give up a little clock, and see how far the voltage can follow it down.
ckp.p.done: About 2.25 GHz runs on 25 W: half the power for a quarter less speed. Power grows with voltage squared, and a slower clock lets the chip run at a lower voltage.
ckp.p.note: A teaching model of a made-up chip: power = activity × capacitance × voltage² × clock, plus leakage (current that flows even when nothing switches). Round numbers, not a real product.
ckp.c.intro: A counter adds one at every tick. Four flip-flops (each holds one bit, and takes a new value only when the clock ticks) hold the count; the gates between them work out the next count, and it must be back at the flip-flops before the next tick.
ckp.c.aria: A counter with a tick every {per} ps and a slowest path of {path} ps: {n} wrong counts.
ckp.c.legend: Above: the slowest path, drawn to its time. The new count leaves the flip-flops, passes two AND gates and an XOR (the carry), and goes back in. Green: a tick that comes just after it ends. Below: twenty ticks.
ckp.c.set.nodeD: How small the factory makes the parts: smaller gates switch faster.
ckp.c.say.ready: Set the clock, then run it: twenty ticks in slow motion.
ckp.c.say.running: Counting. Watch the signal race the next tick.
ckp.c.say.errors: {n} of {of} counts are wrong. Too fast: the clock ticked before the carry had passed through the gates, so the flip-flops stored half-finished sums.
ckp.c.say.top: That is the top safe speed: the slowest path just fits in one tick. Try another process: faster gates, faster clock.
ckp.c.say.top3: That is the top safe speed: the slowest path just fits in one tick. Real 3 nm processors run far slower than this tiny counter, because their slowest paths are much longer and power limits them.
ckp.c.say.above: Still counting right, above the predicted limit: the prediction adds up the worst case of every gate, and real designs keep that margin. Push further.
ckp.c.say.counting: It counts right, with time to spare. Push the clock faster: where does it break?
ckp.c.hint: Watch the line of the next tick against the end of the slowest path. The top safe speed is where the tick lands in the green, just after the path ends.
ckp.c.done: Top speed with no wrong count, at two processes: the slowest path sets the clock. Smaller gates switch faster, so the same counter runs at a faster clock.
ckp.c.note: A teaching model: one fixed delay for each gate, no wire delay, no change of voltage or temperature. Real chips check millions of paths.
game.ch.sig-heart.t: A heartbeat on a coin cell
game.ch.sig-heart.goal: Catch a clean heartbeat for under 20 µW. Which part of the chain eats the budget?
game.ch.sig-heart.why: A phone, a watch or a patch on the skin only knows the world through chips like these: a tiny voltage is made bigger, measured many times a second and turned into numbers. Every number has to be kept or sent, and that costs energy.
game.ch.sig-bearing.goal: Sample a motor's vibration too slowly and watch the warning tone vanish; find the slowest rate that keeps it.
game.ch.sig-bearing.why: A car listens to its own parts. A bearing that starts to fail adds a faint, fast tone to the motor's hum. A chip that measures too rarely does not just miss it: it reports a slower wave that was never there.
game.ch.reg-jobs.goal: Find the best power supply for a fitness band, a phone processor, a precise sensor and a radio.
game.ch.reg-jobs.why: No chip runs straight from a battery. A power chip stands between them and holds the voltage steady while the load jumps. How it does that decides how long the battery lasts, how hot the board gets and how clean the supply is.
grow.island-adc: a listening post on the phone island, its roof stepped like a converter's levels
grow.island-sensor: a test stand at the car works, where a sensor listens to a turning wheel
grow.island-reg: a power house on the phone island, with coils that hold the voltage steady
ana.intro.sig-heart: A heartbeat reaches the skin as about a thousandth of a volt. An amplifier makes it bigger (its gain). A converter measures it many times a second (each measurement is a sample) and rounds it to one of its levels (more bits, finer levels). A radio sends every bit.
ana.intro.sig-bearing: A sensor on a motor feels it shake: a slow hum and, on top, a faint tone at {f} Hz ({f} swings a second), the first sign of a failing bearing. A converter measures the shaking many times a second (each measurement is a sample). Gain is how much the signal is enlarged first; bits set how fine the converter's levels are.
ana.intro.reg-jobs: A regulator turns the battery's voltage into the lower, steady voltage a chip needs. A linear one burns the difference as heat. A switching one chops the voltage and smooths it with a coil: little is wasted, but it leaves a ripple, a small fast wobble, on its output.
ana.aria: The signal and its copy. The copy is off by {e}; the chain draws {p}.
ana.legend: Thin line: the real signal. Dots: the samples. Bold line: the copy rebuilt from them. Below: the gap between the two, up to ±{v}% of the signal's height.
ana.g.copy: How far the copy is off
ana.g.slowest: The slowest rate that keeps it
ana.hint.alias: Aliasing: you sample slower than twice the fastest part of the signal, so fast detail turns into a slow wave that is not there.
ana.hint.clip: Clipping: the gain pushes the signal past the converter's range, so the peaks are cut off. Lower the gain.
ana.hint.levels: The signal uses only a few of the converter's levels. More gain fills the range, so each bit counts.
ana.hint.quality: The copy is not close enough yet: more bits make each step finer, more samples follow fast changes.
ana.hint.power: Good copy, but too hungry. Which part of the bar is biggest?
ana.hint.done: Done. Can you go cheaper still?
ana.b.slower: The warning tone is kept. Sampling faster costs power: can a slower rate still keep it?
ana.b.edge: The tone is kept here. Is this really the slowest? Look at what one step slower does.
ana.b.won: Kept here, and lost one step slower: this is the edge.
ana.done.sig-heart: A clean heartbeat under 20 µW. Most of what you saved is radio: every bit you keep has to be sent.
ana.done.sig-bearing: The slowest rate that keeps the 1.2 kHz tone: just over twice its frequency.
ana.done.reg-jobs: Each job got the regulator that suits it: the best one differs from job to job, for a reason.
ana.nudge.sig-heart: Look at the bar of power: which part draws the most, and what decides how much it has to send?
ana.nudge.sig-bearing: Watch the line of tones while you move the sampling rate. Where is the edge, and on which side of it is the warning tone?
ana.nudge.reg-jobs: Try all three on each job. One may fail for a reason you can read. Of those that work, compare what reaches the chip and how many parts it takes.
ana.note: A teaching model with round numbers, not any product. Real chains also filter before sampling, compress what they send and sleep between measurements.
ana.tone.lost: The warning tone lies past half the sampling rate and is folded back.
ana.tone.kept: The warning tone lies below half the sampling rate.
ana.tone.far: half the rate is off this line
ana.tone.ghost: Tones from slow (left) to fast (right). Past half the sampling rate nothing can be told apart: the warning tone shows up as a tone at {v} Hz that is not there.
ana.tone.ok: Tones from slow (left) to fast (right): the motor's hum, and further right the warning tone. It lies below half the sampling rate, so it is seen where it is.
ana.reg.aria: Battery, regulator and chip: {e}% of the energy reaches the chip, {h} becomes heat.
ana.reg.ldo.d: burns the difference as heat; parts: {n}
ana.reg.buck.d: chops, then smooths with a coil; parts: {n}
ana.reg.both.d: the big step, then a clean-up; parts: {n}
ana.job.wearable.why: A fitness band, asleep 95% of the time.
ana.job.cpu.why: A phone processor running flat out.
ana.job.nearly.why: A radio fed from a supply only a little higher than it needs.
ana.reg.draw2: It draws {a} for {pa}% of the time and {b} in short bursts.
ana.reg.tol: Its supply may wobble by {v} at most.
ana.reg.cool: The regulator may give off {v} of heat at most.
ana.reg.flow: Of every 100 units of energy from the battery, {e} reach the chip and {h} become heat.
ana.reg.start: Pick a regulator to put between the battery and the chip.
ana.rh.dropout: The input must be higher than the output by at least the regulator's dropout.
ana.rh.ripple: Too much ripple: the switching leaves more on the output than this load can tolerate.
ana.rh.heat: Too hot: a lot of heat in one small part. The extra voltage has to go somewhere.
ana.rh.best-ldo: The best choice here. The input is barely above the output, so a linear regulator wastes almost nothing and needs no coil.
ana.rh.best-buck: The best choice here. Switching wastes far less power than burning the voltage difference as heat.
ana.rh.best-both: The best choice here. The buck does the big step efficiently; the small LDO after it removes the ripple.
ana.rh.works: It works, but another choice is better here. Compare efficiency, heat, ripple and the number of parts.
ana.rh.first: It works. Is it the best here? Try another and compare.
ana.reg.note: A teaching model with round values. Real regulators vary widely, and many switch to a low-power mode at light loads.
game.ch.quantize.goal: With at least 1 weight in 100 an outlier, fit a 70-billion-weight model in under 40 GB, and keep the signal more than 20 dB above the rounding error.
game.ch.quantize.why: What a language model knows is held in its weights: 70 billion numbers here, and every word it writes means reading all of them from memory. Storing each in 4 bits instead of 16 makes the model a quarter the size, but 4 bits can tell only 15 values apart. What is lost depends on how the weights are spread.
grow.dc-quant: a memory store that keeps the weights in fewer bits
game.ch.token-energy.goal: First see the building at its best: with the chip untouched, bring cooling and the rest of the server under a fifth of an answer's energy. Then get an answer down to half the energy it started with.
game.ch.token-energy.why: A model writes its answer in tokens, pieces of words. Each token costs energy at the AI chip, and more around it: power supplies, fans, the network, and the cooling that carries the heat away. Which of these is worth working on depends on where the energy really goes.
grow.dc-token: a meter yard that reads where each answer's energy goes
game.ch.prefill.goal: On one Rubin chip with a 70-billion-weight model, find how long a prompt must be before reading it takes as long as writing a 270-token answer.
game.ch.prefill.why: A language model reads your prompt in one pass, all its tokens (pieces of words) side by side. It writes its answer one token at a time, and each token needs a pass through every weight. So a long question can cost less time than a short answer.
grow.dc-prefill: a hall that reads a prompt at once and writes word by word
srv.q.intro: Quantization rounds each weight to the nearest value a short number format can hold, after dividing by a scale so that the biggest still fits. An outlier is a rare weight far bigger than the rest. 20 dB means the weights stand ten times above the rounding error.
srv.q.aria: The weights as trained, a bell curve, and as stored at {bits} bits each: steps. {zero} of the weights are stored as zero.
srv.q.x: a weight's value (1 = an ordinary weight)
srv.q.legend: Grey: the weights as trained. Line: as stored; every weight in a step becomes the one value marked below it. Red: the weights that become zero.
srv.q.legendBlock: Grey: the weights as trained. Line: as stored in a typical block; every weight in a step becomes the one value marked below it. Red: the weights that become zero.
srv.q.legendFine: The steps are too fine to see: stored and trained weights lie on one line.
srv.q.mapAria: Every setting tried: the memory its weights take, against how far the signal stands above the rounding error.
srv.q.mapLegend: Each dot is a setting you have tried; the large one is where you are. The green corner is the goal.
srv.q.verdict.lossless: Practically lossless: the rounding error is far below the noise in training.
srv.q.verdict.small: Small error. With careful calibration, models usually keep their accuracy.
srv.q.verdict.noticeable: Noticeable error. Models need fine-tuning or finer-grained scaling to cope.
srv.q.zeros: {v} of the weights collapsed to zero, because the biggest weight sharing their scale stretched it.
srv.q.is16: A 16-bit format reaches far enough by itself, so it takes no scale.
srv.q.hint: One big weight sets the scale for every weight that shares it. What if fewer weights shared each scale? And what do the scales themselves cost?
srv.q.done: Only FP4 with one scale for every block of 16 weights works: 39.4 GB and about 20.5 dB. One scale for all the weights lets a few large outliers crush every small weight to zero. Small blocks keep each scale local, at the cost of half a bit a weight.
srv.q.note: A teaching model: {n} sample weights from a bell curve, rounded by each format's own rules. The layers of a real model differ from each other.
srv.e.aria: The energy of one token: {a} reaches the AI chip, {s} goes to the rest of the server and its network, {c} to cooling and power losses.
srv.e.legend: A band's thickness is its energy. The bar at the left is what comes in from the grid; its dashed outline is where it started.
srv.e.set.pue: PUE: watts the building draws for each watt its computers use
srv.e.set.overhead: Rest of the server and its network, on top of the chip
srv.e.say.same: An answer costs what it did at the start.
srv.e.say.less: An answer now costs {v}% less than at the start.
srv.e.say.more: An answer now costs {v}% more than at the start.
srv.e.say.building: The best building you found saved {v}%.
srv.e.hint: Look at which band is thickest. The building can only trim its own bands. An answer's energy is power divided by tokens a second: which of the two can move furthest?
srv.e.done: Even a near-perfect building saves less than a third, because most of the energy was reaching the chip all along. The rest has to come from the chip itself: more tokens out of the same watts. That is why services answer many people at once, and why AI chips are judged by tokens per joule.
srv.e.note: A simple model: the chip's power, plus the rest of the server as a share of it, times the building's PUE (the extra goes to cooling and to losses in the power supply), divided by tokens a second. Here every dial moves freely; in a real hall they are tied to each other.
srv.p.intro: Reading (prefill) keeps the chip's arithmetic busy with every token at once. Writing (decode) waits, for each token, while memory hands over every weight.
srv.p.aria: One request in time: reading the prompt takes {read}, then writing the answer takes {write}.
srv.p.legend: Block: the whole prompt, read at once. Stripes: the answer, token after token (one stripe: {k}).
srv.p.say.prefill: Reading takes longer: the chip's arithmetic is the limit.
srv.p.say.decode: Writing takes longer: memory is the limit.
srv.p.say.times: Token for token, reading is {v} times faster than writing.
srv.p.say.chips: The model is too big for one chip's memory, so it is spread over {n}.
srv.p.hint: Compare how fast one token is read with how fast one is written. How many times longer than the answer must the prompt be to even that out?
srv.p.done: It takes a prompt of about 77,000 tokens. Reading works on all the prompt's tokens at once, so the chip computes at full speed; writing produces one token at a time and waits for memory each time. Token for token, reading is about 280 times faster.
srv.p.note: A simple model: reading uses half of the chip's top arithmetic speed; each written token takes as long as reading every weight from memory. The chips' speeds and memories are their makers' own figures.
seek.tap: Tap the parts, on the picture or here. Each has something to notice.
seek.found: This is where the question above starts. Follow it, or keep looking.
seek.kept: Found. It is kept in your log.
seek.server.find: Find the one part of this server that does the sums.
seek.server.fans: Six fans across the front. They run for as long as the server does.
seek.server.accelerator: Only this chip does the arithmetic. Everything around it brings it numbers, power or cold air.
seek.server.memory: The memory sits close beside the chip. The nearer it is, the sooner numbers arrive.
seek.server.network: These links tie this server to the others in the rack, so many machines can work on one job.
seek.phoneboard.find: Find where most of the heat starts.
seek.phoneboard.soc: The processor makes most of the board's heat, in a spot about the size of a fingernail.
seek.phoneboard.pmic: The power chip warms too: each change of voltage loses a little energy as heat.
seek.phoneboard.modem: The modem works hardest when the signal is weak, and gets warmer then.
seek.phoneboard.storage: Storage draws power mostly while it reads or writes, so it often stays the coolest chip here.
seek.gate.find: Find what decides which rule this gate follows.
seek.gate.gates: Each switch gate is one input. It crosses both silicon strips, so it turns one switch on and another off.
seek.gate.diff: The two silicon strips hold two kinds of switch: one kind turns on with a high voltage, the other with a low.
seek.gate.metal: The switches here are the same kinds as in every other gate. What differs is how these wires join them.
seek.campus.find: Find where the electricity comes in.
seek.campus.halls: Each hall is full of racks and has its own cooling and power, so a campus can grow one hall at a time.
seek.campus.cooling: The machines on the roofs carry heat away. Nearly all the electricity that comes in leaves again as heat.
seek.campus.substation: Here the grid's high voltage is stepped down for the halls. Everything on this campus runs on what comes in here.
seek.hall.find: Find what ties these racks to each other.
seek.hall.racks: Row after row of the same cabinet, each full of computers built alike.
seek.hall.hotaisle: Cold air goes in at the fronts of the racks and comes out hot at the back, into this closed aisle.
seek.hall.trays: The network's cables run in these trays, from rack to rack. They are what let many machines share one job.
seek.rack.find: Find where the calculating is done.
seek.rack.switch: Every server in the rack is cabled to this switch, and through it to the rest of the hall.
seek.rack.servers: Each shelf is a computer built around a few large chips. This is where the calculating happens.
seek.rack.power: The hall's electricity becomes the low, steady voltage the boards need here. Every server above draws on it.
seek.board.find: Find where this board's sums are done.
seek.board.package: The chip that does the sums sits in this package. Everything else on the board feeds it power or numbers.
seek.board.lid: The metal lid protects the chip and spreads its heat into the heat sink that sat on top.
seek.board.powerstages: Each of these small blocks turns the board's supply into the very low voltage the chip runs on. There are many, because the chip draws so much current.
seek.accel.die: Copies of one compute tile, side by side. Each copy does the same steps on different numbers.
seek.accel.hbm: Each tower is memory chips stacked on top of each other, set right beside the die so numbers have only a short way to travel.
seek.accel.base: The die and the memory towers stand on one base. Layers of wiring inside it join them, and carry every connection out to the board.
seek.handset.find: Find where the day's energy comes in.
seek.handset.screen: When it is lit, the screen spends more of the battery than any other part. Most of the day it is dark, and the chips inside go on working.
seek.handset.antenna: The radio keeps in touch with the network even while the phone sleeps, and works harder when the signal is weak.
seek.handset.cable: Everything the phone did today came out of one battery. This cable fills it again, usually overnight.
seek.chip.find: Find the blocks that do the work.
seek.chip.cores: Each compute block fetches numbers, calculates and passes results on. None of them sees the whole job.
seek.chip.cache: Memory on the chip itself. A number kept here arrives far sooner than one from the memory outside.
seek.chip.io: Every number the chip works on comes in, and every result goes out, through these circuits at its edge.
seek.chip.clock: One tick, carried on these wires to every part, keeps the whole chip in step.
seek.phone.board: All the phone's computing is on this one small board, at the top. Most of the rest is battery.
seek.phone.battery: The battery fills most of the phone. Every other part has to fit around it.
seek.phone.camera: The lenses gather light and the sensor records it. What the photo finally looks like is worked out afterwards, by the chip.
seek.phone.antenna: Parts of the metal frame are the antennas: the case itself reaches out to the network.
seek.soc.find: Find the district built for the sums AI needs.
seek.soc.cpu: Big cores and small ones: the phone moves work between them, to save energy when the work is light.
seek.soc.gpu: Many small, identical cores that draw the screen's pictures, all working at once.
seek.soc.npu: This district does the multiplications AI needs, many at a time, for less energy than the other cores would use.
seek.soc.isp: The camera unit gets the picture first, straight from the sensor, before any other district sees it.
seek.soc.cache: Every district reads and writes here, so work can pass from one to another without leaving the chip.
seek.car.controllers: Small computers sit all over the car, in hot places and cold ones, each in charge of one job.
seek.car.wiring: Cables carry power and messages between the control units, through the whole car.
seek.car.sensors: Cameras and radar watch the road and pass what they see to the computers.
seek.car.battery: The floor of the car is its battery, and a control unit of its own watches every cell.
seek.car.motor: The inverter beside the motor switches large currents on and off, many thousands of times a second.
seek.car.wheels: Everything the computers decide ends here, as braking, steering and turning wheels.
seek.ecu.mcu: This small chip makes every decision in the unit, running the same program again and again.
seek.ecu.connector: Every signal from the car's sensors, and every command out, passes through this plug.
seek.ecu.drivers: These big switches carry the real current. They do only what the small chip tells them.
seek.mcu.find: Find where the program is run.
seek.mcu.cores: Two cores do the same work in step. If their answers ever differ, something has gone wrong.
seek.mcu.flash: The program lives here, and stays when the car is switched off.
seek.mcu.sram: The numbers being worked on right now live here, and are lost when the power goes.
seek.mcu.periph: Signals from the sensors arrive here and become numbers the cores can use.
seek.scanner.find: Find where the light is made.
seek.scanner.source: A laser hits drops of molten tin, and the flash of light it makes is what prints the chip.
seek.scanner.mirrors: This light is swallowed by glass, so there are no lenses here: only mirrors, polished extremely smooth.
seek.scanner.mask: The pattern of one layer, drawn larger than it will be printed, like a stencil.
seek.scanner.stage: The wafer moves under the light and stops at each chip in turn, exactly in place.
seek.scanner.vacuum: This light cannot travel through air, so the inside of the machine is pumped empty.
seek.die.find: Find the part that does your chip's work.
seek.die.cores: Your chip's cores: the same pattern on every chip of this wafer.
seek.die.pads: Small metal squares round the edge: the only way in or out for every signal.
seek.die.probes: Needles touch the pads and test the chip while it is still on the wafer.
seek.die.scribe: The lane between chips. A saw will cut along it, and nothing here is kept.
seek.block.cells: Every standard cell in a row has the same height, so a program can line them up like books on a shelf.
seek.block.sram: Each cell of this grid holds one bit, and only for as long as the power stays on.
seek.block.wires: The wires run on many layers above the cells, so they can cross each other without touching.
seek.switch.find: Find the part that turns this switch on and off.
seek.switch.gate: Its voltage decides whether current crosses the sheets. It controls the flow without joining it.
seek.switch.channel: The current flows through these thin sheets of silicon, with the gate wrapped around them on every side.
seek.switch.oxide: This skin is so thin that the gate's voltage acts straight through it, yet almost no current crosses it.
seek.switch.source: The moving charges enter the sheets here. Source and drain look alike: which is which is set by the voltages on them, not by their shape.
seek.switch.drain: The charges leave the sheets here and go on through the wires above.
seek.atom.lattice: Each silicon atom holds on to four neighbours, in the same pattern over and over.
seek.atom.dopant: One atom of another element among the silicon. Its spare electron, or the one it lacks, is what lets current flow here.
seek.atom.electrons: The electrons drift from atom to atom, and that drift is the current.
seek.atom.boundary: Close up, the switch's insulating skin is only a few rows of atoms. Electrons can slip through a wall that thin.
joule.q: One answer from an AI costs energy. Where does it all go, and how far down could we bring it?
joule.job: One answer from a 70-billion-parameter language model, 500 words long: a multiply-add for every weight for every word.
joule.pulled: {lever}: the whole answer changed by {v}%, and so did every level below and above.
joule.other: The other sides it pays on: {s} s for an answer, and an accuracy of {db} dB.
joule.keep: Keep this plan as an attempt
joule.here: of one answer go here, at the {level}
joule.at.building: Pumping out the heat and converting power. It pays for everything below it once more.
joule.at.rack: The network between machines: every answer's numbers cross it.
joule.at.board: Fetching the model's weights from memory for every word, and the host machine around the chip.
joule.at.chip: Moving numbers through the chip's own memory, on their way from far memory to the blocks.
joule.at.block: Reading the two numbers of every multiply-add from registers right beside it; with compute in memory, summing them in the arrays instead.
joule.at.gate: The arithmetic itself: the only part the answer needs.
joule.at.switch: Current that leaks through switches that are off, for as long as the answer takes.
joule.at.atom: The least physics asks for: the bits the arithmetic erases, at room temperature.
joule.lever.home.d: Memory chips on the board, stacks of memory beside the chip in its package, or the whole model in on-chip memory.
joule.lever.batch.d: Each weight fetched is used once for every user served at the same time.
joule.lever.precision.d: Fewer bits move fewer bytes and need smaller multipliers, and add rounding noise.
joule.lever.clock.t: Clock, at the lowest voltage that runs
joule.lever.clock.d: A slower clock runs at a lower voltage; below the lowest voltage, leakage takes over.
joule.lever.cim.d: Sum the weights inside the memory arrays where they are stored, with converters at the edge.
joule.lever.adcBits.d: How finely the arrays' sums are read back: each bit doubles the converters' energy.
joule.lever.pue.d: Power use effectiveness: the building's energy over the machines'. Liquid cooling brings it nearer 1.
joule.lever.optics.d: Plugged-in optical modules, or optics packaged beside the switch chip.
joule.map.aria: {n} attempts, by the energy of one answer against the time it takes. Yours is the ring.
joule.map.d: Each dot is an attempt, by its energy (down is less) and its time (left is quicker). The large dots are on the frontier: nothing beats them on energy, time and accuracy at once. Your plan is the ring.
joule.map.none: No attempts in the ledger yet. Yours can be the first.
joule.model: The budget engine, on a 45 nm ruler: the shares and the directions hold, the joules are for comparing ideas. Nobody votes; the engine scores every attempt.
joule.offer.d: This question runs through a puzzle: where does the energy of one answer go, level by level?
joule.no.job: The job needs operations, bytes and reuse as numbers.
joule.no.home: Where the weights live: on the board (dram), beside the chip (hbm) or on the chip (sram).
joule.no.precision: Bits per number: fp16, fp8 or fp4.
joule.no.clock: The clock must be between 0.5 and 4.5 GHz.
joule.no.volt: The voltage must be between 0.5 and 1.1 V, and high enough for the clock.
joule.no.batch: Users served together: a whole number from 1 to 4,096.
joule.no.cim: Compute in memory is on (true) or off (false).
joule.no.pue: The hall's power use effectiveness: from 1 to 3.
joule.no.optics: Optics between machines: plug or cpo.
ledger.no.plan: The plan is not one the puzzle's engine can run: check each lever's value.
ledger.state.beaten: beaten on energy, time and accuracy
ledger.rec.attempt: An attempt at where the energy goes · {wh} Wh an answer
api.open.puzzle: A puzzle that runs through every level: read the budget, pull the levers, and submit a plan that beats the frontier.
api.tool.energy: The energy puzzle: for a plan (where the weights live, bits per number, clock, users served together, compute in memory, cooling, optics), the energy of one AI answer at every level of a data centre, from the hall to the atom, split into computing, moving data and heat, with the floor physics sets, the time an answer takes and its accuracy. Also the levers, each with the lab where it is played, and the attempts so far.
api.tool.attempt: Submit an attempt at the energy puzzle: a plan, scored by the budget engine and checked by the ledger (a plan the engine can run, new among the attempts). It comes back as the entry's file and the link that opens it in a pull request; nothing is posted.
api.arg.plan: The plan: any of home (dram, hbm, sram), precision (fp16, fp8, fp4), clock (GHz), volt (V, or null for the lowest that runs), batch (users), cim (true or false), adcBits, pue and optics (plug, cpo). Left out: the starting plan's value.

machines.ui.go: Pick a need, and build a machine for it from shared blocks, with an agent beside you
machines.ui.title: What would you build if machines were assembled from shared blocks, for one person and one need?
machines.ui.lead: There is no standard computer here. Pick a need, then choose the form of each block: as software it can change at any time, as a circuit it runs far cheaper but is fixed once made, as liquid hardware it is a fabric rewired after it is made, and as new matter it is made of something beyond today's chip. Or let an agent assemble it, and decide for yourself.
machines.ui.energy: the energy of the same machine made all as circuits
machines.ui.changes: parts that can still change after it is made
machines.ui.reset: Start again: every part a circuit
machines.ui.agentLead: The agent tries every way to make this machine, in every place it could be made, keeps those that follow the grammar and meet the need, and shows the ones no other beats on energy, change, exactness and days a try at once. It decides nothing.
machines.ui.tried: Tried {tried} machines: {valid} pass, and {front} are beaten by no other.
machines.ui.decide: Which one is right depends on what the machine is for. That is your call, not the agent's.
machines.ui.blocksLead: What everyone shares instead of a standard machine: what flows in and out of each block, the forms it can take, and how it is checked.
machines.ui.note: How it is scored: for the same work, software costs about 500 times a circuit made for it (a general-purpose chip against a custom one for video, Hameed et al.), and new matter costs what its claims say, from in products down to guesses, shown as a range and never below the energy floor. Each part's share of the work is a choice of the model, so the energy is always this machine against itself, never in joules.
machines.rule.kind: {part}: a wire joins two different kinds of port
machines.rule.fed: {part} has an input that nothing feeds
machines.rule.core: {part} runs as software, but no core made as a circuit is there to run it
machines.miss.change: {part} must still change after the machine is made: make it software or new matter
machines.miss.exact: {part} must be exact, and new matter is not
machines.check.open: Open in the community's plan: anyone can design it
machines.check.partly: Partly built in the community's plan
machines.check.engine: Waits for an engine that can check it
machines.check.lab: Checked by one of the lab's engines
machines.block.sensor.d: Turns a signal from the world, such as sound, smoke or light, into numbers.
machines.block.learner.d: Numbers in, numbers out, shaped by numbers it has learned: a filter, a detector, a guide.
machines.block.memory.d: Keeps numbers until they are needed.
machines.block.counter.d: Counts ticks: a clock for when to wake up and what to do next.
machines.block.voter.d: Three copies answer and the majority wins, so one fault cannot change the result.
machines.block.parity.d: Says whether a number arrived with one bit flipped.
machines.block.core.d: A RISC-V core: it runs any block given to it as software.
machines.need.hearing.d: Tiny, all day on one small battery
machines.need.hearing.why: Its filter has to be tuned to each person's hearing, so it must still change after the machine is made.
machines.need.wildfire.d: Ten years in a forest, no service
machines.need.wildfire.why: Nothing has to change once it is out there: what matters most is the battery.
machines.need.rover.d: Far away, cold, hit by radiation
machines.need.rover.why: Its guide has to take updates from Earth, and its voter and core must be exact, because radiation flips bits out there.
invent.ui.lead: New matter may not exist yet, so every kind rests on claims, and every claim says how sure it is: in products, shown in a lab, or a guess. Guesses are allowed and labelled; physics sets the floor.
invent.ui.none: No part is made of new matter yet. Choose the hexagon on a part that can take it to see the claims behind each kind.
invent.ui.range: If the guesses hold: {low} the energy of a circuit. If they fail: {high}.
invent.matter.cim.d: Numbers held and multiplied where they are stored.
invent.matter.light.d: Multiplies by sending light through a mesh of tiny tunable splitters.
invent.matter.spikes.d: Neurons that fire only when something happens, as in a brain.
invent.matter.reversible.d: Logic that can run backwards and take back the energy of each step.
invent.matter.living.d: Lab-grown neurons on a chip that learn, kept alive.
invent.claim.cimArray: A crossbar multiplies where the numbers are stored; its energy, converters included, comes from the lab's compute-in-memory engine.
invent.claim.cimNoise: No two devices are quite alike, so the answers are close, not exact.
invent.claim.lightReal: Processors that compute with light are installed in research computing centres.
invent.claim.lightNoise: Light drifts in phase, so the answers are close, not exact.
invent.claim.lightCheap: Multiplying in light costs a tenth of what a circuit spends.
invent.claim.lightConvert: Turning numbers into light and back costs twice what the light saves.
invent.claim.spikesReal: Spiking systems with over a billion neurons have been built.
invent.claim.spikesEvents: A spiking part spends energy only when something happens, so a quiet need costs little.
invent.claim.spikesCost: Each spike costs three times a circuit's step.
invent.claim.revChip: A reversible test chip took back part of its energy: the same logic used about 30% less.
invent.claim.revFree: Taken back almost completely, a step would cost almost nothing.
invent.claim.liveReal: A computer with living neurons on a chip is on sale today.
invent.claim.liveBrain: Living neurons compute as cheaply as a brain, which runs on about 20 watts.
invent.claim.liveSupport: Keeping the cells alive costs a hundred times what they save.
invent.wall.floor: A claim hit the floor: no step can cost less than erasing the bits it must erase, so the guess stops there.
ledger.no.machine: There is no such need to build a machine for.
ledger.no.machineFails: This machine does not follow the shared grammar or does not meet its need yet.

machines.rule.fab: {part} cannot be made where you chose: pick another place, or another form
machines.ui.days: days for one try: from a design to a part to test
fab.ui.lead: Software changes the same day. Everything else has to be made first, and where it is made sets how many tries fit in a year.
fab.ui.none: Nothing in this machine needs making: its parts are software or bought ready-made. A try takes a day.
fab.ui.grown: Living matter is grown from cells, not made in a fab: how long a try takes is not known here.
fab.ui.guessDays: {low} days a try, if the guess holds
fab.ui.setup: a line costs {x} of a giant fab to set up
fab.ui.note: Energy here is counted as if every part were made at 45 nm. Lines this coarse cost more energy per step: try here, then make the one that wins at a giant fab.
fab.name.giant.d: The fabs that make today's chips: every form, at the finest lines, and months for each try.
fab.name.small.d: Minimal Fab: a line of small tools on half-inch wafers, with no cleanroom.
fab.name.flexible.d: Thin-film circuits printed on plastic: slower and larger than silicon, made in days.
fab.name.desk.d: Chips made at home, or by machines a factory of fabs turns out: a try a day, perhaps.
fab.claim.giantDays: 18 to 26 weeks from a finished design to tested wafers.
fab.claim.giantCost: The yardstick: what every other line is set against.
fab.claim.smallReal: In use: no cleanroom, half-inch wafers, sold for prototyping.
fab.claim.smallCost: A hundredth to a thousandth of the cost of a giant fab, its makers say.
fab.claim.smallDays: A few days to two weeks a try: a guess; we found no source.
fab.claim.flexDays: Under 48 hours a run; under a week to tested wafers.
fab.claim.flexWeek: The same source sets silicon at 18 to 26 weeks.
fab.claim.flexCost: A hundredth of the cost of a standard fab, its maker says.
fab.claim.deskReal: One person made a chip of 1,200 transistors in a garage, at 10 µm.
fab.claim.deskFab2: A company is building a factory that makes small fabs and the tools in them.
fab.claim.deskDays: A day to a week a try: a guess.
fab.claim.deskCost: A ten-thousandth of a giant fab: a guess.
invent.claim.liveGrown: Grown from cells, not made in a fab: how long a try takes is not known.
curve.ui.title: How fast do ideas get better here?
curve.ui.lead: Every attempt someone keeps for this need joins the curve, in order: each dot is one attempt, and the line is the best energy so far. Nobody votes; the engine scores each one.
curve.ui.none: No attempt at this need has been kept yet. Yours would be the first point.
curve.ui.noLaw: {n} attempts so far. With three, and one that beats the first, the curve has a law.
curve.ui.law: Each time the attempts double, the best falls to {x} of what it was.
curve.ui.pace: At the pace of your machine, {tries} tries a year, doubling the {n} attempts so far alone would take {time}.
curve.ui.paceNever: Your machine rests on a try whose days are not known, so nobody can say how fast it moves the curve.
curve.ui.many: That is why it is a lab: many people and many agents, each trying in parallel, double the attempts much faster than one.
curve.law.moore: Moore's law counts years: chips double every two years or so, and keeping that pace now takes more than 18 times the researchers of the early 1970s.
curve.law.wright: Wright's law counts things made: cost falls by a share each time the total made doubles, and it forecast 62 technologies best.
curve.law.lab: This curve counts attempts: the best design falls each time the attempts double. More attempts, faster tries, more ideas.
curve.ui.keepLead: It joins the curve at once, as yours. To put it in the ledger, open it on GitHub as a new file in a pull request.
curve.ui.cannot: Make a machine that follows the grammar and meets its need, and it can join the curve.
machines.miss.keep: {part} must reshape as fast as its job changes, and this form is too slow
machines.need.radio.d: The signals around it change in nanoseconds
machines.need.radio.why: The signals it hunts change faster than most hardware can be rewired: finding them and pulling them out must reshape every 100 nanoseconds, and pulling them out must be exact.
liquid.kind.fpga.d: An FPGA: a grid of tiny lookup tables and switches, rewired by loading a new configuration.
liquid.kind.cgra.d: A coarse-grained array: small arithmetic units whose wiring changes on every tick of the clock.
liquid.kind.goal.d: The goal: a fabric that reshapes in 50 nanoseconds at nearly a circuit's energy.
liquid.note.fpgaArea: About 35 times the area of a custom chip for the same logic, and 3.4 to 4.6 times slower.
liquid.note.fpgaWhole: Rewiring the whole chip took 3.8 seconds; rewiring part of it, 209 milliseconds, or 324 microseconds through the chip's own port.
liquid.note.cgraChip: A test chip had 28.6 times the power efficiency of an FPGA platform; against a circuit made for the job, no source gives one figure.
liquid.note.goalAim: DARPA's aim: processors that reconfigure within 50 nanoseconds. Nobody has shown it yet.
liquid.ui.lead: A fabric rewired after it is made: exact like a circuit, changeable like software. It pays in energy for the switches that make it flexible, and in the time it takes to rewire, when it does no work.
liquid.ui.mapAria: How fast each part of this machine can reshape, against its energy compared with a circuit made for the job
liquid.ui.corner: fast to reshape and costs like a circuit: nothing is there yet
liquid.ui.everyKey: parts that must change have to be right of the line
liquid.ui.none: No part is liquid yet. Choose the drop on a part that is logic to see the fabrics.
liquid.ui.energy: {x} the energy of a circuit made for the job
liquid.ui.fallback: If the guesses fail, a guessed fabric is no better than an FPGA: its energy and its time to rewire.
liquid.ui.evolve: When a fabric rewires itself, who designed it? In 1996 evolution rewired an FPGA to tell two tones apart, and the circuit worked in ways nobody could fully explain.

home.title: Make a chip, from an idea to a billion switches.

home.wafer.note: Every speck of dust kills the chip it lands on. Same dust, bigger chips: fewer of them survive.
home.q.line: Where should the line fall between fixed structure and fluid adaptation?
home.q.moore: What will be the next Moore's law?
home.q.geo: Is the ceiling of intelligence fundamentally a geometry problem: packing parts close to communicate, while spreading them apart to stay cool?
home.q.vn: How can a whole be more reliable than its parts?
home.q.sutton: Why does more computing keep beating cleverer ideas of human design, and will it always?
home.q.dig: Where does the digital world end and the physical begin?
home.q.trust: What can trust rest on when a system is too complex to inspect or test?
home.q.copy: To think efficiently as a brain, must a machine give up the power to copy its mind?
home.q.nat: If almost anything in nature can compute, what if anything remains beyond computation?
home.q.human: When AI makes generating options free and tools spread to everyone, what can only humans bring, alone and together?

frame.at.line.building.q: One hall, thousands of machines, rearranged by software every day. Which parts should be fixed, and which should keep changing?
frame.at.line.building.note: The jobs and the network of a hall are rearranged by software all the time; the chips inside are fixed the day they are made.

frame.at.eff.rack.note: For every joule a chip uses, the server and the building around it use more: fans, power conversion and cooling.
frame.at.geo.rack.q: Pack more accelerators into one rack and they talk faster, and cook each other. How close is too close?
frame.at.geo.rack.note: Many racks for AI now carry so much heat that air cannot remove it, and liquid is brought to the chips.
frame.at.eff.board.q: Most of an answer's energy is spent on this board, fetching numbers from memory. Make it cheaper, and what happens to the total?
frame.at.eff.board.note: In the energy puzzle, moving data across the board is the largest share of one AI answer's energy.
frame.at.perfect.board.q: The same board, built a million times. Which copy fails first, and why?
frame.at.perfect.board.note: Chip and board grow by different amounts as they warm, and the joints between them flex every time.
frame.at.geo.chip.q: The memory sits a few millimetres from the chip, and every number the cores use has to make that trip. Is the trip the real cost?
frame.at.geo.chip.note: Reading 16 bits from memory chips costs about 3,500 times the energy of a 16-bit add, on a 45 nm chip.
frame.at.eff.chip.q: Make each answer cheaper and people ask for more. On this chip, what is the energy of one answer spent on?
frame.at.eff.chip.note: Most of an AI answer's energy goes to fetching the model's numbers from memory, not to the arithmetic.
frame.at.physics.block.q: Sum the numbers where they are stored, as currents in a memory array. Let physics do the arithmetic, noise and all?
frame.at.physics.block.note: Compute in memory adds stored weights in place; its catch is noise, and converters that cost more for every bit.
frame.at.eff.block.q: Slow the clock where nothing is changing and the same work takes half the power. What will the saving be spent on?
frame.at.eff.block.note: Switching energy grows with the square of the voltage, and a slower clock can run at a lower voltage.
frame.at.dig.gate.q: Push a messy signal through this gate and a clean 1 comes out. Where does the mess go?
frame.at.dig.gate.note: Each gate restores its signal to a clear 0 or 1, so noise does not pile up from one gate to the next.
frame.at.vn.gate.q: Three copies of this gate, and a vote. When is a crowd of unreliable parts more reliable than one good one?
frame.at.vn.gate.note: A vote among three copies outvotes one fault; von Neumann showed in 1956 that reliable machines can be built from unreliable parts.
frame.at.physics.switch.q: Hot silicon leaks, and leaking makes more heat. Fight it with a lower voltage, or put the physics to work?
frame.at.physics.switch.note: Leakage through switches that are off grows quickly as the silicon warms.
frame.at.dig.phoneboard.q: A heartbeat is a smooth wave, but the chip keeps only numbers. How many numbers a second are enough to still call it the same heartbeat?
frame.at.dig.phoneboard.note: Between the skin and the processor sits a converter: the last place on the board where the signal is still a voltage and not yet a number.
frame.at.dig.ecu.q: A failing bearing makes a real tone; a chip that samples too slowly reports a slower tone that was never there. Where did the made-up wave come from?
frame.at.dig.ecu.note: Sampling slower than twice the highest frequency folds fast tones into false slow ones, so a filter must remove them before the converter sees them.
frame.at.vn.soc.q: Billions of transistors, some of them sure to be weak. How does a phone's chip keep working for years anyway?
frame.at.vn.soc.note: Chips carry spare memory rows and codes that catch errors, and are tested and sorted after making, so a weak part is swapped out or the chip is sold to run a little slower.
frame.at.vn.mcu.q: A car maker wants almost no failed chips in a million. How can a small controller be more reliable than any one of its parts?
frame.at.vn.mcu.note: Safety controllers run two cores in lockstep that compare every result, with memories that correct their own flipped bits, so one fault is caught before it acts.
frame.at.perfect.deposit.q: A film that misses the bottom of one trench in billions leaves a hole. Grow it one layer of atoms at a time, or accept some gaps and design around them?
frame.at.perfect.deposit.note: Atomic layer deposition coats every surface evenly by adding one layer of atoms per step, and pays for it by being far slower than other ways of growing a film.
frame.at.eff.print.q: A brighter light source makes each wafer cheaper to print. Will cheaper printing mean less power spent, or many more chips made?
frame.at.eff.print.note: Almost all the electricity that drives an EUV source is lost before light reaches the wafer, so every gain in the source goes straight into more wafers an hour.
frame.at.physics.implant.q: Heat repairs the crystal and switches the dopants on, and the same heat lets them wander. Fight the spreading, or put it to work?
frame.at.physics.implant.note: A laser can heat the surface for a tiny fraction of a second: long enough to switch dopants on, too short for them to spread far.
frame.at.vn.ship.q: In a fleet of millions of chips, faults rare for one chip happen every day. How can the fleet give right answers when some of its chips do not?
frame.at.vn.ship.note: Large fleets have found chips that quietly return wrong results; operators now test chips while they run and retire the ones that slip.
game.ch.chef.goal: The processor is a chef who gets faster every round; memory is the pantry. Keep the chef cooking at every level of chips, from one wire to a data centre, without spending more than each level allows.
game.ch.chef.why: Information weighs nothing, but it always rides on something physical: a charge on a wire, a pulse of light. So moving one bit costs energy, time, wires, money and a chance of error, and nothing outruns light. Chips have grown faster much more quickly than memory has, so a faster chip waits more of its time for data.
grow.dc-pantry: a pantry stacked on a kitchen, its door lit
q.bits.q: If information weighs nothing, why does moving it cost so much? Play it as a kitchen: keep the chef busy.
ledger.no.chef: There is no such level in the kitchen.
ledger.rec.chef: An attempt at Keep the chef busy: {level} · the chef waits {wait}% · {e} J an answer
mb.trip.intro: Send one bit from memory to the arithmetic and watch what it costs. Then move the memory: on the chip, stacked on it, beside it, across the board, or in another machine reached by light.
mb.trip.look: Fetch two numbers: {f}. Add them: {a}. {k}× more to fetch.
mb.trip.wireShare: {v} of the bit's energy is spent on the way, not in the memory
mb.trip.note: Energies from the same 45 nm table as Follow the joule: right in direction and share, high for today's chips. Capacity counts every wire; money is the price of a gigabyte kept there.
mb.at.near.d: Memory on the same chip (SRAM, fast memory built from switches), a millimetre from the arithmetic: cheap to reach, but it takes costly chip area.
mb.at.stacked.d: Memory stacked straight on top of the chip and joined through thousands of tiny vertical wires: short and wide, but the heat has further to go.
mb.at.beside.d: A stack of memory chips beside the processor in the same package (HBM), joined by thousands of wires through a silicon bridge.
mb.at.board.d: Memory chips on the circuit board, about ten centimetres away: few wires, and every bit is pushed out of one chip and into another.
mb.at.rack.d: Memory in another machine two metres away, reached through a fibre: light costs the same few picojoules whether it goes a metre or a hundred, but it adds time.

mb.wall.lightD.other: At light's own speed this trip lasts {n} ticks of a 3 GHz clock; the bit takes {m}.

mb.wall.kLight.one: At light's own speed the pantry is {n} of the chef's ticks away; a fetch takes {m}.
mb.wall.kLight.other: At light's own speed the pantry is {n} of the chef's ticks away; a fetch takes {m}.

mb.k.intro: Each round the chef cooks faster; the pantry hardly speeds up. Pull the levers, then serve five rounds. A level is cleared when, in the last round, the chef waits no more than the goal and an answer costs no more energy than it allows.
mb.k.aria: {level}, round {r}: the chef waits {wait} of the time; {e} an answer.
mb.k.note: A small model, fair enough to compare plans and never wrong in direction: the chef grows faster as processors did against memory (Wulf and McKee, 1995); prices and sizes are the model's own. Every lever's catch is in the engine, src/engines/bits.js.
mb.lv.wire.q: Fetching two numbers costs far more than adding them. Why?
mb.lv.wire.who: The chef is a chip's arithmetic; the pantry is memory on the far side of the same chip, a wire away.
mb.lv.chip.q: Why does a faster chip spend more of its time waiting for data?
mb.lv.chip.who: The chef is a processor; the pantry is memory chips across the board.
mb.lv.stacked.q: What if the work were brought to the data: memory stacked on the chip, or cooking inside it?
mb.lv.stacked.who: The chef is an AI chip; the pantry is a stack of memory beside it in the package.
mb.lv.light.q: Past some distance a wire loses to light. Where is that distance?
mb.lv.light.who: The chef is a processor; the pantry is a pool of memory a metre away, in another box.
mb.lv.dc.q: AI chips sit idle much of the time, waiting for numbers. How much of that wait can be won back?
mb.lv.dc.who: The chef is an AI chip answering one person: every number of the model is read once for each word it writes, and used once.
mb.lv.brain.q: A brain's signals crawl compared with a chip's, yet it thinks quickly on very little power. How does it keep its wires short?
mb.lv.brain.who: The chef is a group of neurons; the pantry is what other parts of the brain hold, a nerve fibre away.
mb.lv.team.q: Everyone on a team knows something. Why does sharing it take so long, and what helps?
mb.lv.team.who: The chef is a person at work; the pantry is what a colleague across the building knows.
mb.lever.closer.catch: Less room: memory on the chip takes space from the chef.
mb.lever.wider.catch: More wires and more money, and the chip's edge holds only so many.
mb.lever.shelf.catch: A cache must guess what comes next; a wrong guess fetches for nothing.
mb.lever.stack.t: Stack the pantry on the kitchen
mb.lever.stack.catch: The heat is harder to get out, so the chef slows down.
mb.lever.light.catch: Turning bits into light and back costs energy, near or far.
mb.lever.cim.catch: Computing in memory: the answers become approximate.
mb.lever.closer.brainC: Cells packed together leave less room for others.
mb.lever.wider.brainC: Every fibre costs room and energy to keep.
mb.lever.shelf.brainC: A local memory must guess what will be needed.
mb.lever.stack.brainC: A tighter fold is harder to cool.
mb.lever.light.brainC: Signals race along, but the wrapping costs room to grow.
mb.lever.cim.brainC: Answers come out roughly right, not exact.
mb.lever.closer.team: Sit near the people you ask
mb.lever.closer.teamC: Desks near one team are far from another.
mb.lever.wider.teamC: More people in the room cost more hours.
mb.lever.shelf.teamC: Notes must guess what will be asked; most are never read.
mb.lever.stack.teamC: The noise slows everyone down a little.
mb.lever.light.teamC: Every call takes minutes to set up.
mb.lever.cim.team: Let the one who knows do it
mb.lever.cim.teamC: It gets done their way, not quite as asked.

game.ch.flaky.t: Six flaky parts, one reliable chip
game.ch.flaky.goal: Build each block of a small chip once, three times or five times with a voter, so the whole chip goes wrong fewer than 5 times in 100 runs, on no more than 32 units of floor.
game.ch.flaky.why: In 1956 John von Neumann asked how a machine can be more reliable than the parts it is made of. One answer: make copies and take the majority. A vote outlasts any one bad copy, but copies cost area and power, and the voter is a part too. Space probes and the safety chips in cars still vote today.
grow.studio-vote: three copies of a block and their voter beside the studio, one copy lit red and the answer still green
game.ch.mortal.t: Learn on one chip, copy to a thousand
game.ch.mortal.goal: Make a network at most 30% as costly per answer as an all-digital one, right at least 95% of the time on its first chip, and at least 90% on every copy.
game.ch.mortal.why: A brain computes with very little energy because what it learned is the physical state of its own cells, and so it cannot be copied. A digital computer copies perfectly, and pays to move every bit. Chips that compute with analog cells sit between the two: cheaper, but each chip is a little different. Geoffrey Hinton calls computing whose knowledge dies with its hardware "mortal".
grow.way-mortal: a chip that learned, warm on its plinth at the Lab, and a row of its copies, each lit a little differently
rd.aria: The chip's blocks drawn as their copies and voters; the whole chip is right {v} of the time.
rd.legend: Each tile is one copy of a block, as wide as the block is big; the wedge is the voter, which passes on what most copies say. On the right, how often each block still gives a wrong answer.
rd.r.none: Run a thousand chips to watch the copies fail and the votes hold.
rd.intro: Every block of this chip sometimes gives a wrong answer, the big ones most often, and the chip is right only when every block is. A block can be built three or five times, with a voter that takes the majority. Each copy takes floor, and the voter can be wrong too.
rd.msg.met: The whole chip is now right more often than its worst part alone. Copies of the flaky blocks outvote their bad moments; the small, steady blocks were left alone.
rd.msg.worse: Voting made the {b} worse: it rarely goes wrong on its own, and the voter adds a chance of its own to go wrong.
rd.msg.big: Too much floor: the copies no longer fit the chip. Which blocks gain least from their copies?
rd.msg.close: The whole is already more reliable than its worst part. Not yet enough: where would one more copy help most?
rd.msg.bare: Built once each, the whole chip goes wrong far more often than any one part: every flaw adds up.
rd.msg.more: Better. The blocks that fail most still pull the whole chip down.
rd.hint: A vote only pays where a block goes wrong much more often than the voter. Start with the blocks that fail most, compare what three and five copies buy for their floor, and leave the steady small blocks as they are.
rd.done: A whole more reliable than its parts, for a price in floor, power and speed. With smaller switches every part grows flakier, and the question comes back harder: where does voting stop paying, and what else can a whole do?
rd.note: A teaching model with round numbers: each copy goes wrong at random, independently of the others, and the voter is one part with its own small chance of being wrong. Left out: faults that hit every copy at once (a shared supply, a shared clock, the same design mistake), the time the vote takes, and codes that fix errors with fewer copies.
mo.aria: A network on a chip, its first chip right {own}% of the time and its copies {copied}%.
mo.fig.first.sw: the first chip, written from software
mo.legend: A grid is a layer kept as bits; a wave, a layer kept as analog cells. Each copy is coloured by how often it answers right: green at 90% or better, amber above 85%, red below. The line on the energy bars is the goal.
mo.t.energy: goal: at most {v}% of all bits
mo.intro: A small network reads a sensor and answers. Kept as bits, its numbers copy exactly, but every answer moves them, and moving bits costs energy. Kept as the state of analog cells, it computes for far less, but no two cells, and no two chips, are quite alike.
mo.learn.software: In software, then written to the chip
mo.cal: Each copy relearns a little on its own chip
mo.msg.met: Cheap, right on its own chip, and copyable, at the price of a few minutes of relearning on every copy. A brain pays the other price: it never copies at all.
mo.msg.digital: All bits: exact, copyable, and every answer pays to move every number.
mo.msg.costly: Still costly: most of each answer's energy goes on the layers kept as bits.
mo.msg.brain: Like a brain: it learned around its own chip's quirks and works well there, but on any other chip those quirks are wrong. What it knows dies with the chip.
mo.msg.blind: Learned in software, it copies faithfully, but it never saw this chip's quirks, so every chip, the first too, answers worse.
mo.msg.more: Close. One of the three still falls short.
mo.hint: Try the three ways of learning at a high analog share, and watch the copies change colour. Learning on the chip fits one chip; learning in software fits none exactly. What if each copy fits itself?
mo.done: Copyable and cheap, but only by relearning on every copy, and the more is analog, the longer that takes. Is that a machine that copies its mind, or one that grows a new one each time from a shared start?
mo.note: A teaching model with round numbers, not measurements: analog layers about twelve times cheaper per answer than bits, every analog cell off by about 10%, and accuracy falling with the square of the noise. Left out: cells that drift with time and heat, the cost of the converters at each layer's edge, and networks trained to tolerate noise.
game.ch.dieread.goal: Say what kind of chip each die photo comes from, four times, and find every kind of block on one die by its texture alone.
game.ch.dieread.why: Engineers read die photos to learn what a chip is for, check what they were sold, and find where a chip failed. Memory, logic, repeated cores and hand-drawn circuits each have a look under the microscope, and where the area goes gives the chip's purpose away. Trusting a chip starts with being able to see inside it.
grow.test-xray: a microscope in front of the test house, a die lit on its stage
xray.type.dram.clue: Huge, extremely dense arrays split by thin strips: almost the whole die is memory.
xray.type.pixels.clue: A vast field of tiny coloured squares: one light-sensitive pixel each, under red, green and blue filters.
xray.type.adc.clue: A long, thin strip of identical columns along the pixel array: one converter for each column of pixels.
xr.why.mcu: Most of the area is memory (flash for the program, SRAM to work in) and analog circuits that talk to the outside world. The processor itself is a speck.
xr.why.phone: A block for each job: big and little processor cores, graphics, an AI engine, image and video engines, and memory links along the edge.
xr.why.gpu: A sea of identical cores, with a band of cache across the middle and links to the stacked memory down both sides.
xr.why.dram: Almost the whole die is memory arrays, with a thin strip of control logic and a row of pads down the middle.
xr.why.camera: Most of the area is the pixel array, with a row of converters above and below it, one for each column of pixels.
xr.ask: What kind of chip is this?
xr.wiring: That is wiring and spacing between the blocks.
xr.g.found: Every block found on one die
xr.cleared: Dies read to the last block: {n}
xr.aria: A photo of a chip's die, its blocks drawn with the textures they have under a microscope.
xr.done: You can read a die: memory as a regular grid, logic as fine noise, copies of one tile, hand-drawn shapes, and the share of area that tells what a chip is for. A die photo is one way to check a chip; what is hidden below the top layer, or in its design, is the harder part.
